name: Cayman Islands
summary_text: The Cayman Islands decriminalised same-sex intimacy in 2001 through an Order in Council imposed from London after the local legislature declined to act, and the reform left an unequal age of consent in its wake.  In August 2009 members of the United Kingdom's Foreign Affairs Committee criticised the Cayman Islands' draft constitution for deliberately excluding gay rights, calling the omission deplorable and warning that the drafting could leave the territory's courts affording citizens less protection than Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights requires. The Foreign and Commonwealth Office answered that the draft's list of discrimination grounds was open-ended.  Relationship recognition moved through the courts rather than the statute book. Grand Court Chief Justice Anthony Smellie struck down the prohibition on same-sex marriage in March 2019; the Court of Appeal overturned that ruling in August 2019, restoring the statutory ban.  Recognition then arrived through immigration administration. In December 2020 immigration authorities recognised the overseas same-sex marriage of Paul Pearson and Randall Pinder, who had wed in Ireland, and the Court of Appeal held that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds. Overseas marriages therefore carry immigration effects in the Cayman Islands even though no local route to marriage exists.  Public visibility is high in the tourist-facing environment. Around 600 people, including the premier, the governor, ministers and MLAs, joined the Cayman LGBTQ Foundation's first Pride parade on 7 August 2021, with broad official participation. Organisers asked participants to refrain from excessive displays of affection as a condition of the public-space route.

sources.title: Grand Court Ruling - Day and Bodden v Government, 29 March 2019 by Chief Justice Anthony Smellie
sources.documents: Declared same-sex marriage ban unconstitutional; key marriage-equality ruling later stayed
sources.detail: Lawsuit lodged June 2018 by Chantelle Day and Vickie Bodden, oral arguments February 2019, decision 29 March 2019; no URL shown

name: Cyprus
summary_text: Cyprus does not criminalise same-sex sexual activity. Consensual conduct was decriminalised in 1998 after the European Court of Human Rights held in Modinos v. Cyprus that Criminal Code section 171 violated the right to private life. The offence of promoting homosexuality was lifted in 2000 and unequal ages of consent were equalised in 2002. The universal age of consent is now 17. The former military exclusion of homosexuals has been removed. In the northern part of the island, deputies voted on 27 January 2014 to repeal the provision that punished homosexual acts with up to five years’ imprisonment.  Cypriot law provides no general prohibition of discrimination based on gender identity. The 2004 Equal Treatment in Employment and Occupation Law prohibits only sexual-orientation discrimination in employment. Gender identity remains absent from equal-treatment grounds.  Article 99 of the Penal Code, titled incitement to violence or hatred due to sexual orientation or gender identity, punishes intentional public threatening, insulting or offensive urging or incitement, orally or in writing, of violence or hatred on those grounds with imprisonment not exceeding three years or a fine. The provision originated in the October 2013 Penal Code amendment and was carried into Law 87(I)/2015 as a public hate-speech offence. Parliament raised the fine for sexual-orientation or gender-identity hate speech in October 2024 to 10,000 euros. Separate 2017 provisions are reported as punishing incitement based on sexual orientation with up to five years’ imprisonment and a fine up to 10,000 euros.  Law 31(I)/2017 provides that prejudice-based motivation operates as an aggravating factor in sentencing.  Enforcement of hate-crime protection is inconsistent. Eleven complaints were examined in 2015 with five criminal prosecutions reported as pending trial. Reports of incitement against LGBT people have at times resulted in no police or legal action, most notably when committed by clergy of the Greek Orthodox Church. Police failed to establish a hate-crime motive after a February 2019 attack on a gay man in Nicosia, and no police action was reported after a second Nicosia incident four months later. An LGBTI non-governmental organisation assessed the legislation as fragmented and inadequate, finding that many LGBTI persons remain not open about sexual orientation or gender identity and do not report homophobic violence or discrimination.  Conversion practices are banned and criminalised under Law 39(I)/2023, adopted by parliamentary vote on 25 May 2023.  No gender-recognition law is in force. The national report prepared for the Universal Periodic Review stated that legislation for correcting registered sex for adults and minors was in preparation and would require only a Registrar decision without prior medical intervention or psychiatric reports. A bill discussed after President Nicos Anastasiades met Accept-LGBT Cyprus in November 2017 would have allowed persons over 18 to change legal gender on the basis of self-determination without diagnosis, hormonal treatment or sex reassignment surgery. On 10 June 2019 four parents of transgender children urged speedy adoption after months of stalling and delay. The legal gender recognition bill was approved by the Council of Ministers in September 2022 with a first parliamentary reading in November 2022 and remained pending in 2024.  Queer Cyprus documents a separate recognition practice in the northern part of the island. That process is described as self-determination without psychiatric or surgical gatekeeping and as explicitly including recognition of non-binary identities.  Marriage remains legally recognised only as a union between one man and one woman, with no same-sex marriage recognition. A civil-union law granting several marriage rights and benefits passed on 26 November 2015 by 39 votes in favour, 12 against and 3 abstentions and took effect on 9 December 2015. Adoption remains reserved to heterosexual couples only.

sources.title: Modinos v. Cyprus - European Court of Human Rights (1993)
sources.documents: Foundational decriminalization ruling; Court ruled section 171 of Cyprus Criminal Code violated right to private life under European Convention on Human Rights.
sources.detail: Cited in text as 'Modinos v. Cyprus, at the European Court of Human Rights' by Alexandros Modinos, architect/gay rights activist; Convention ratified by Cyprus in 1962; Articles 171-174 of Chapter 154 of Cypriot Criminal Code. No URL visible in article text.

sources.title: Equal Treatment in Employment and Occupation Law 2004
sources.documents: Cyprus anti-discrimination employment law explicitly forbidding discrimination on basis of sexual orientation; basis for workplace protections.
sources.detail: Cited as 'Equal Treatment in Employment and Occupation Law 2004 (Greek: Ο Περί Ίσης Μεταχείρισης στην Απασχόληση και την Εργασία Νόμος του 2004)'; designed to comply with EU Employment Framework Directive of 2000. No URL visible.
